response.consequence: With credential sync enabled, the stored credentials never record an expiry, so isExpired treats them as expired. Every request re-calls the sync endpoint. The stored refresh_token is overwritten with the literal "refresh_token". Zoom's later code, which reads fields such as expires_in from the parsed data, is also affected.
response.explanation: The schema keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are not wildcard patterns. Each evaluates to the same literal string "[object Object]". The second key overwrites the first, so the schema reduces to `access_token: string` plus an optional "[object Object]" property. Zod objects strip unknown keys by default. When credential sync is enabled, safeParse therefore returns data containing only `access_token`. The expiry field (`expiry_date`, `expires_in` or similar) and any other returned properties are dropped. parseRefreshTokenResponse then fills `refresh_token` with the placeholder "refresh_token". Callers such as office365calendar and zoomvideo merge `tokenResponse.data` into the stored credential. That stored credential ends up with no expiry and a fake refresh token. The "any number property is the expiry" comment is not implemented.
response.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses nonsensical computed keys and strips the expiry field

response.consequence: On sync-enabled installs, refreshed credentials lose their expiry information and their real refresh token is replaced by the placeholder string "refresh_token". Subsequent refreshes then fail or tokens are treated as never expiring. Validation also never checks for a numeric expiry as the comment intends.
response.explanation: Zod schema objects have no custom toString. `z.string().toString()` and `z.string().optional().toString()` both return "[object Object]". The two computed keys are therefore the same key, and the second one overwrites the first. The schema becomes `{access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown.optional()}`. The "assume any numeric property is the expiry" requirement is never enforced. Zod's default object parsing strips unknown keys, so the parsed data keeps only `access_token`. `expiry_date`, `expires_in`, the real `refresh_token` and every other field are dropped. The next lines then see `refresh_token` as missing and set it to the literal "refresh_token". When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, callers get `data` with no expiry and a bogus refresh token. The Google caller stores the result as the credential key, which would persist those values.
response.title: Computed keys collapse to "[object Object]"; the sync-mode schema strips expiry and refresh_token

response.consequence: Every Salesforce calendar service construction fails after the refresh request. The Salesforce integration breaks, and the refreshed token is never persisted. If the refresh token rotates, the stored credential is left stale.
response.explanation: The change adds `prisma.credential.update(...)` in SalesforceCalendarService.getClient. The file never imports or declares `prisma`; a grep finds only this use. The import block (lines 1-20) has no `@calcom/prisma` import. After a successful token refresh, execution reaches this line and throws a ReferenceError (or fails type-check). The same function also builds the jsforce Connection with the old `credentialKey.access_token` instead of the freshly refreshed token, and it calls the token endpoint on every service construction.
response.title: Salesforce getClient uses `prisma` without importing it

response.consequence: An attacker who can send many requests could in theory recover the shared secret through timing differences. They could then overwrite any user's app credentials. Exploiting this over a network is hard, so the impact is low.
response.explanation: The headline concern is ruled out. APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED in packages/lib/constants.ts:103 is `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, and the handler returns 403 when it is falsy. So the secret and the key are both non-empty whenever the comparison runs, and undefined===undefined cannot pass. The empty-key fallback is also unreachable. What remains is that the secret is compared with `!==` (lines 22-25), which is not constant-time. The compare is also against a header value that may be a string[] or a string, though an array never equals the secret string, so that part is harmless.

other_findings.consequence: A caller who sends a malformed body or an incorrectly encrypted payload gets a generic 500 with no useful error. The 500s also add noise to error monitoring.
other_findings.explanation: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` (line 28) throws a ZodError on a malformed body. `symmetricDecrypt` and `JSON.parse` (lines 55-57) throw on a bad ciphertext or non-JSON plaintext. None of these calls is wrapped in try/catch, so each failure becomes an unhandled 500 instead of a 400.
other_findings.title: Unhandled zod and JSON.parse/decrypt errors give 500s

response.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time !== (fail-open on unset secret is ruled out)

response.consequence: After the first successful token refresh, every Google Calendar credential is overwritten with a malformed key. Later parses of that key throw, so the integration breaks for those users until they reconnect.
response.explanation: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the zod safeParse result object, `{ success: true, data }`. It does not return the parsed data. The Google caller assigns that object to `key` and passes it to `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. The stored key therefore becomes `{success: true, data: {...}}` instead of the credential fields. On the next call, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in googleAuth fails because access_token and the other fields are missing at the top level. In credential-sync mode, refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, so `res?.data` is undefined and `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. In that mode the function cannot work at all. The Office365 caller has the same pattern in a milder form: it checks `.success` on a result that now throws on failure, so the `.success &&` guard is dead code and failures now throw instead of being handled.
response.title: Google refresh persists the whole {success, data} parse result as the credential key
